Named entity recognition is a task that is often complicated by the presence of similar entity types within the same set of potential labels. FGNET, a more complex variation of NER, is characterized by numerous potential labels and a large number of entities with fine-grained subtypes. The challenge lies in distinguishing between these subtle differences. FGNET-RH, a proposed model, leverages the natural representation of hierarchical relationships within the curvature of hyperbolic space to accurately classify entities. The model's effectiveness is demonstrated through its superior performance on the CoNLL2003 dataset, where it outperforms traditional Euclidean-based approaches.

This paper provides upper limits for the Hankel determinants of the second order for functions within the univalent class and more broadly for the starlike functions class, specifically examining their implications for various subclasses.

In a cloud data center, managing virtual machine resources effectively is crucial for optimizing performance and reducing costs. Excessive provisioning of resources leads to increased operational expenses, whereas underprovisioning results in dissatisfied customers. To address this challenge, a novel strategy called Prepartition has been developed to balance the load of virtual machine resources in the cloud data center. The proposed approach utilizes a non-linear optimization model to achieve optimal load distribution and minimize operational expenses. The results of the simulation study demonstrate that Prepartition achieves a 10% reduction in operational expenses, and the results of the real-world deployment show that the strategy can be successfully implemented in cloud data centers.

In game theory, a fundamental challenge is predicting the equilibrium state that arises when multiple self-interacting agents engage in repeated interactions. To address this issue, a novel approach called Fixed Point Networks (FiPNets) is introduced, which utilizes a neural network-based algorithm to forecast equilibrium states directly, without the need for time-consuming simulations. By employing a novel loss function, FiPNets can be trained to ensure its predictions converge to a true equilibrium state, and a new training method called Fixed Point Loss Scaling is developed to enhance the stability of training. Experimental results demonstrate that FiPNets can accurately predict equilibrium states across various game scenarios, and also successfully learn complex dynamic behaviors that emerge during negotiations.

In the context of causal inference, a well-known theorem called the Glicksberg theorem plays a pivotal role, particularly when dealing with data that has multiple dimensions. This theorem helps to establish a crucial link between two different types of mathematical functions, a link that is essential for proving the existence of certain functions in complex systems. Our research delves into the implications of the Glicksberg theorem, specifically focusing on the causal influences that exist between variables, and we derive new, tighter limits on a key concept called Lipschitz constants. These constants measure how sensitive a system is to changes, and they are essential for understanding how information flows through complex systems. Our research also showcases the practical applications of these new limits, particularly when dealing with data that has multiple dimensions, and we provide a detailed analysis of how these limits can be used to solve real-world problems.

This study proposes a method for detecting cyber attacks on linear systems using an predictive approach. When an attack occurs, the system's performance is compromised, but remains concealed from the control system, as stealthy attacks are designed to evade detection. To address this limitation, we develop an online state estimator that utilizes all available sensor data to estimate the system's current state. This estimated state is then used to forecast the system's future behavior, which is subsequently compared to the actual measurements. Discrepancies between the predicted and measured states indicate the presence of an attack. Our approach is validated through a case study on a linear system, demonstrating its effectiveness in detecting cyber attacks.

This research introduces GAE-ISumm, an unsupervised graph-based summarization model tailored for Indian languages, capable of generating concise summaries across diverse domains within these languages. By leveraging GATs to create sentence representations and a GAT-based self-attention mechanism to capture inter-sentence relationships, GAE-ISumm produces summaries as node prediction tasks on artificially constructed graphs. Evaluations conducted on datasets in Hindi, Bengali, and Malayalam demonstrate that GAE-ISumm outperforms existing methods, including rule-based, neural, and ensemble approaches, across multiple metrics. Furthermore, an analysis of the model's behavior and limitations is provided. The code and datasets associated with this research are publicly accessible via https://github.com/ashishkumar1999/GAE-ISumm.

A s-ring is a structured framework that generalizes group concepts, and we will explore a specific type of s-ring known as Cohen-type s-rings. These s-rings will be characterized by three main criteria: they must have the same number of isotope pairs, belong to the same class of s-rings, and possess a particular type of mapping called a pseudo-isomorphism that acts as a non-identity permutation. We will demonstrate the existence of multiple distinct s-rings that meet these criteria, and we will also identify a specific condition under which any s-ring with less than 100 elements can be classified as a Cohen-type s-ring.

Recent studies have linked a notable trend of stars exhibiting increased acceleration to the dark matter hypothesis. This led to a need to verify the underlying cause of this phenomenon, which involved a small group of stars. We aimed to obtain more precise estimates of the masses and distances of the companions orbiting five stars, which previously showed acceleration. Using Gaia's data on the stars' movements and the previously established relationships between the stars and their companions, we calculated the masses and distances of the companions. Our analysis revealed that the companions' masses are likely between 0.01 and 0.1 solar masses, and the distances are within a few hundred astronomical units. These findings support the conventional explanation for the observed acceleration, which attributes it to mass loss from the stars rather than dark matter.

Deep learning models, particularly those based on variational autoencoders, have achieved remarkable success in solving inverse problems. However, the traditional variational autoencoder approach can be computationally expensive due to its maximum likelihood estimation method. To address this issue, we introduce a new regularization technique that simplifies the computational process by replacing the likelihood with a least squares loss, thereby reducing the complexity of the problem and enabling efficient computation.

A significant concern in the Internet of Things (IoT) is the security of smart homes, particularly the monitoring of devices such as smart locks, security cameras, and other equipment. To address this challenge, we have developed a security system that leverages blockchain technology and a location-based approach to monitor smart home devices. This solution utilizes a blockchain platform, such as Hyperledger Fabric, to safeguard data and employs a localization method to pinpoint the location of compromised devices. Furthermore, we have designed a private mobile application to alert users to suspicious activity and facilitate remote management of their smart devices.

A recent breakthrough in deep learning-based quantization of channel variables has led to the development of DL-based quantizers that can be integrated with Gray coding to enhance the performance of modulations like QPSK and 8-QAM in single-input single-output systems. However, this approach is not directly applicable to modulations like 16-QAM and 64-QAM, which employ cross-mapping between bit patterns and symbol values. To address this limitation, a new quantization method is proposed that combines the benefits of both conventional and Gray-coded quantizers through the use of a neural network-based cross-mapping function. Simulation results demonstrate that this new method achieves performance comparable to the best existing schemes while offering a more efficient trade-off between complexity and performance.

For a given planar graph, creating a layout where it appears to hang from the top of a page, with y-coordinates increasing along a designated root path, results in an "upward planar drawing." We've developed two techniques to efficiently create such layouts for specific types of graphs, specifically 2-tree and series-parallel graphs, by parameterizing them with the size of these structures. These algorithms have significant implications for other parameterized problems, including the detection of planar structures and graph embedding, allowing for more efficient solutions in non-outerplanar 2-tree graphs and series-parallel graphs, respectively.

Crowdsourcing tasks often result in ambiguous data, which can be leveraged to gauge respondents' confidence in their answers. By analyzing the spread of probability distributions derived from softmax outputs, we can measure uncertainty in crowdsourced data. To address the challenges posed by noisy data, we've developed a multi-model ensemble approach that incorporates various algorithms, including Support Vector Machines, Random Forests, and Neural Networks, to identify and mitigate data inconsistencies.

We examine the stability of norm-regular half-smooth transfer operators associated with half-flow maps on compact surfaces that have the boundary fixed. Under certain conditions, we demonstrate that the norm can be decreased arbitrarily by adjusting the half-flow map's parameters. In contrast, our investigation reveals that the norm is unbounded when considering generic half-flow maps.

A method is developed to construct efficient, small size covering arrays that are strength 2, using modified Seidel matrices, which are then utilized to create the arrays through a specific linear algebra technique. It is proven that these constructed arrays are optimal in several instances.

We examine the possibility of a quantum strategy outperforming a classical one in a non-local game. Specifically, we focus on games played with noisy versions of the Bell state. While determining whether any quantum strategy exists for these games remains an open question, we find that deciding whether a given binary strategy exists is a solvable problem.

A previous study by Albrecht et al. showcased the effectiveness of a guided genetic algorithm in automatically reproducing network crashes, but their results were based on a highly optimized version of the algorithm. This research aims to evaluate whether a simpler version of the algorithm can still perform well in the same task. We modified the algorithm by removing its guidance system and replacing a sophisticated fitness function with one that is more basic. The results indicate that the simplified algorithm is still capable of producing valid reproductions, albeit with some limitations. These findings suggest that the basic concepts of the algorithm are sound and that further research could lead to more efficient crash reproduction tools.

The complex interplay between vortices in high-temperature superconductors is a topic of significant interest. Theoretical models suggest that vortex interactions can lead to the formation of ordered grid structures. To explore this phenomenon, we conducted an experiment using the pseudogap regime of a Bi$_2$Sr$_2$CaCu$_2$$\textrm{O}_{8+\textrm{x}}$ superconductor. Our study involved applying magnetic fields and currents to the material and measuring the resulting vortex dynamics. The observed behavior of the vortices revealed a previously unreported phase transition, where the material's vortex configuration changed from a four-fold grid to a more complex structure. The findings provide valuable insights into the complex physics of high-temperature superconductors and may have implications for the development of new materials with improved superconducting properties.

Our investigation focuses on the thermal photon emission process and its potential to measure the flow characteristics of the quark-gluon plasma created in heavy-ion collisions. By utilizing a microscopic kinetic theory, we have calculated the momentum distribution of photons, taking into account the evolution of the quark-gluon plasma through its early stages up to the point of chemical freeze-out. Our results indicate that the anisotropic flow ($v_2$) of photons exhibits a notable sensitivity to the early-stage properties of the plasma, particularly its shear viscosity. Specifically, we have found that the $v_2$ ratio of photons at low momenta ($p_T$) is less than that of hadrons, and this disparity becomes more pronounced with a higher shear viscosity. Furthermore, we have discovered that the $v_2$ ratio of photons to dileptons increases with a higher shear viscosity, and this effect is also more pronounced at higher $p_T$. These findings suggest that thermal photons can serve as an effective tool for understanding the transport properties of the quark-gluon plasma.

We've developed a comprehensive framework to analyze magnetic orders in both kagome and triangular lattices with four distinct spin sites per unit cell. This results in 16,416 unique 120-degree order possibilities, which we've broken down into a smaller set of 100 fundamental patterns. These fundamental patterns can be combined to create all possible orders, revealing that only 10 of these patterns are truly unique, while the rest can be derived through symmetry operations. Our method is applicable to any system exhibiting 16,416 possible magnetic orders, such as those with kagome and triangular lattices.

Large-scale A/B testing is widely used in tech companies to analyze the impact of product changes on user behavior. However, drawing conclusions from multiple tests under dependent conditions can lead to inflated false positive rates. To address this, we developed a new approach that uses False Discovery Rate control to quantify and limit the proportion of incorrect results among the significant findings. Our method relies on the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure, which has been shown to be effective under dependent conditions. To further enhance performance, we developed a dependent robust estimator for the positive correlation rate and proved its reliability. Additionally, we demonstrated the effectiveness of our approach through real-world data analysis and simulations.

In the context of General Relativity, the universe's expansion is represented by the FLRW metric, which describes the expansion of space. This effect is distinct from the expansion of objects within space, as it is often misinterpreted. The expansion of space is a geometric property, not a process, and objects embedded within it do not expand. The FLRW metric models the expansion of space using the scale factor a(t), which is a function of time. This factor is typically normalized to a(t0) = 1 at the present time, and its rate of change determines the expansion velocity of galaxies. The expansion velocity is directly proportional to a galaxy's distance from us, as described by the Hubble constant H0. The expansion of space is driven by the Friedmann equations, which model the expansion of the universe. The first Friedmann equation relates the expansion rate to the density of matter and energy within the universe, while the second Friedmann equation describes the acceleration of the expansion. The expansion of space is a fundamental concept in cosmology, and it has been confirmed by various observations, including the redshift of distant galaxies.

The long-standing anomalies in the muon's magnetic moment and W boson mass have been addressed in this study by utilizing the mass splitting between charged Higgs bosons and W bosons to determine the mass splitting in a type-X two-Higgs-doublet model. By applying the complex mass scheme to the model, the one-loop corrections to W boson self-energy were calculated and the Muon magnetic moment was computed. The analysis revealed that a mass difference of approximately 300 GeV between charged Higgs bosons and W bosons can account for the discrepancies in both muon $g-2$ and $W$ mass measurements.

In software engineering, locating relevant information within a large codebase is a significant challenge. To overcome this, researchers have developed techniques that utilize natural language processing to analyze user requests and extract key concepts from them. These techniques rely on accurate parsing of the requests, but current methods struggle with ambiguous or complex queries. To address this limitation, we propose an innovative approach that leverages the power of crowdsourcing to automatically refine and improve query understanding. By incorporating a large dataset of crowd-sourced knowledge, our system can identify and incorporate additional concepts into the query, thereby enhancing its accuracy. Our experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in identifying and incorporating relevant concepts from the crowd-sourced dataset.

This study focuses on quantifying entrainment in conversational speech, a phenomenon where speakers adjust their speech patterns to align with their conversation partners. Existing methods for measuring entrainment rely on manual annotation of dialogue, which is time-consuming and costly. In contrast, this research proposes a novel, unsupervised approach that leverages pre-trained deep neural networks to automatically detect and measure speaker adjustments in real-time, without the need for extensive annotation. The proposed metric focuses on aligning the speech patterns of individual speakers within a conversation, and its effectiveness is evaluated using a large dataset of naturalistic dialogue. The results demonstrate that this approach can accurately detect a wide range of speaker adjustments, including adjustments in speech rate, pitch, and other acoustic features.

Researchers in the field of planetary science require versatile web-based tools to efficiently analyze and present data obtained from various imaging and spectroscopic techniques.  To address this need, a set of open-source web tools, known as RCSEDv2, has been developed.  These tools enable researchers to visually explore and analyze data in a comprehensive manner, utilizing interactive 2D and 3D visualization, statistical analysis, and advanced spectral analysis techniques.  By incorporating features such as inter-presentation correlation, outlier detection, and principal component analysis, RCSEDv2 provides a robust framework for researchers to uncover meaningful patterns and insights from their datasets.  The tools have been successfully applied to a variety of datasets, including those from the Mars Hand Lens Imager and the James Webb Space Telescope, demonstrating their effectiveness and versatility in real-world scenarios.

This paper presents a self-supervised learning approach for temporal action segmentation that relies on body pose information. The proposed method, called Self-supervised Co-occurrence Action Analysis (SSCAP), utilizes an unsupervised objective function that identifies distinct temporal action segments based on the co-occurrence patterns of body pose information. The SSCAP model generates self-supervised temporal representations that accurately identify and delineate action segments. The model's effectiveness is demonstrated through accurate action segmentation on the UCF101, DUT-OMDB, and THUMOS14 datasets, as well as unsupervised action segmentation performance on an action recognition benchmark.

This study aims to formulate a comprehensive theory of pentaquark states, including those with hidden charm and those with open charm, as well as those containing odd-odd isospin combinations. These states are considered to be hadronic molecules composed of meson-meson pairs, with the di-meson system bound by meson exchange forces. The results of this investigation include the determination of the masses, binding energies, and internal structures of these states, as well as the prediction of their production and decay characteristics. The internal structures of these states are found to be complex, with significant components of both $S$-wave and $D$-wave meson-meson configurations. The predicted masses of these states are in good agreement with experimental findings. The study also predicts the production of these states in various reactions, including $\bar{B}B$ and $\bar{B}K$ scattering, as well as their decays into multiple final states. The predicted decay widths of these states are also calculated and compared with experimental findings.

This paper presents the outcomes of a research study that compared the efficacy of a novel feedback mechanism in teaching software testing. We investigated whether an innovative inquiry-based technique, in which students identify and rectify flaws in a program, is more effective than conventional methods where the instructor directly provides the correct solution. Our results indicate that students who were asked to find and correct the program's errors on their own demonstrated a deeper understanding of the testing process and a higher level of engagement. Additionally, this paper outlines the methodology and findings of our research study.

Deep learning models trained on limited data often struggle with generalization when deployed in diverse environments. Domain adaptation seeks to overcome this limitation by leveraging domain-specific information from the target domain. Unlike traditional approaches requiring costly data collection, our proposed method utilizes an existing video dataset to perform adaptation without needing additional target data. This novel approach, called semi-supervised hypothesis shift, shifts the adaptation burden from the domain level to the hypothesis level, allowing the model to adapt by incorporating video-based hypotheses. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach across multiple datasets, with significant improvements in zero-shot domain adaptation scenarios.

Deep space missions can be significantly accelerated by utilizing advanced propulsion systems, specifically high-performance engines like air-breathing ramjets and gas-core reactors. These reactors, which are a subject of extensive theoretical and numerical research, are being investigated for their potential in long-duration space exploration. A key challenge in this research lies in accurately modeling the complex interactions between gas dynamics, heat transfer, and nuclear reactions. By employing a multi-physics approach, this study aims to develop a comprehensive numerical framework that can simulate these coupled phenomena, ultimately enabling the design of efficient reactor-based propulsion systems.

We introduce a novel neural network approach for accurately determining the spatial coordinates of astroparticle interactions within large-scale detector volumes. Building upon the success of deep learning methods in particle physics, our framework integrates a neural network with traditional reconstruction algorithms to achieve optimal results. To enhance accuracy, we leverage knowledge of the detector's physical processes and incorporate it into the network's optimization process. We test this domain-informed method using data from the LUX-ZEPLIN experiment, comparing it to conventional techniques and finding that our method significantly improves interaction localization accuracy.

The number of exoplanet discoveries is increasing rapidly, with researchers now focusing on characterizing the atmospheres of these planets. However, researchers face a significant challenge in analyzing the spectra of these planets, particularly those with the atmospheres of types M and L dwarfs and gas giants. To address this issue, we have developed EXOPLINES, a comprehensive archive of molecular absorption cross-sections for the gases commonly found in these planets. This resource aims to facilitate the analysis of their spectra, with the hope of unlocking new insights into the atmospheres of these celestial bodies.

This paper explores the fundamental concept of grounding in Answer Set Programming, a crucial step for translating logic programs into their semantic interpretations. We outline the core principles and methods for constructing the reduct function, which underpins the grounding process. By examining the essential properties of the reduct, this work provides a comprehensive overview of the theoretical underpinnings of ASP.

In the field of quantum information, a recent breakthrough has been made in the law of quantum resource, a concept that encompasses various theories. This law provides a fundamental understanding of the cost of creating quantum resources, a topic that has been a central issue in the field. This paper aims to address this gap by developing a new theoretical framework that encompasses the principles of the original quantum resource theory. This framework is exemplified by the coherence and discord theories, which have been shown to be consistent with the proposed law. This breakthrough has significant implications for the field, as it opens up new avenues for research and may lead to the development of new quantum technologies.

Statistical models often incorporate parameters to account for uncertainty in data measurements, but these models' predictions are typically not aligned with actual data due to an overestimation of uncertainty. This issue, known as the calibration problem, is prevalent in statistical models. We propose a straightforward method to determine the parameters of a Gaussian model by utilizing the data's empirical distribution function. This approach is versatile and can be applied to various types of data, including continuous, discrete, and censored data. We validate the method's effectiveness through theoretical analysis, simulation studies, and real-world applications.

We develop a novel method for estimating parameters in complex, multivariate time series models that exhibit heavy tails. Our approach relies on a specific mathematical transformation, which allows us to derive explicit formulas for the model's key characteristics. These formulas enable the creation of efficient estimation techniques for multiple model parameters. Our results show that our estimators are reliable and have known error rates, even in difficult scenarios. Our approach is particularly useful for a class of time series models that generalize the widely used Student-t model. Our methods are demonstrated through their application to real-world data, specifically daily stock prices from the S&P500 index.

We introduce an LDPC quantum code that achieves a high rate, has relatively short block and decoder lengths, and can efficiently correct both bit and syndrome errors. The code's rate, relative distances, and block lengths scale with specific power laws, resulting in a decoder with linear time complexity. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our quantum code can be adapted to have any specified rate while maintaining similar performance characteristics.

In a graph, a distance-$r$ dominating set is a collection of vertices, where every other vertex in the graph is within a distance of at most $r$ from at least one vertex in the set. This distance-$r$ dominating set can be considered as a partition of the vertices into groups, where each group has a representative vertex that is within a distance of at most $r$ from all the vertices in that group. This problem is known as the distributed distance-$r$ dominating group problem. This problem has been studied for various values of $r$, and it has been shown that it is possible to find such groups in a distributed manner for certain classes of graphs. This work presents a distributed algorithm that can find a distance-2 dominating group of size at most $100 \ln n$ in a specific class of graphs, and it also shows that it is possible to find such groups of size at most $100 \ln n$ in a specific class of graphs with a specific degree bound. This work also presents a lower bound on the size of the dominating set for some graph classes, and it shows that it is possible to find such dominating sets in a specific class of graphs with a specific girth. This work also discusses the relationship between this problem and other problems in graph theory, and it shows that it is possible to reduce some problems to this problem. This work also presents an open problem for future research.

A theoretical framework is developed to investigate the relationship between bulk and surface properties in disordered topological insulators of a higher dimensionality. This model incorporates the effects of disorder on the unique topological features of these insulators. Based on the established concept of bulk surface correspondence, a simplified equation is derived to predict the topological characteristics of these insulators using information from their bulk and boundary states. This formula is tested using numerical simulations of two-dimensional disordered topological insulators with various topological properties.

Recent searches for supersymmetry at the CMS experiment have yielded no evidence for its existence within specific theoretical frameworks. These studies primarily focused on various Supersymmetry models, setting upper limits on the production cross-sections and excluding certain regions of the model's parameter space at a 95% confidence level.

A novel technique, Bright Field Neural Rendering (BFRN), has been developed to create realistic images of complex objects, specifically objects with bright highlights, by creating a link between a point cloud and image generator. This BFRN model, which uses multiple layers of data, has been found to outperform existing models in creating realistic images of objects with point clouds.

Observations from the SOAR telescope's IRAM interferometer in 2021 yielded 1,000 successful data sets, yielding 750 datasets with high data quality. These observations facilitated the creation of detailed images of 400 binary star systems, with 150 of which were precisely measured for the first time. Notably, the study revealed 50 new binary star systems, with 10 systems displaying unique orbital characteristics.

We explore the interconnections between three distinct concepts: Celestial chiral algebras, a newly discovered relationship between hue-kinematics and soft theorems, and integrable operator product expansions. We begin by examining how celestial chiral algebras can be used to construct and categorize the entire set of celestial operators. We then establish a link between the scaling dimensions of these operators and their conformal weights, which is achieved through a method of calculating correlation functions. We subsequently establish a relationship between the poles in these correlation functions and the structure constants of the celestial chiral algebra. We also establish a duality between hue-kinematics and the integrability of operator products. Finally, we establish a connection between the scaling dimensions of the celestial operators and the universal coefficients in soft theorems, which is achieved through a method of calculating scattering amplitudes. We also establish a relationship between the poles in these amplitudes and the structure constants of the celestial chiral algebra.

A piston wave triggered by a coronal mass ejection was detected in the solar atmosphere using the LOFAR telescope. The wave, moving at approximately 100 km/s, was observed at a height of around 10,000 km above the sun's surface. The piston wave was accompanied by white-light emission, caused by the shock wave heating the surrounding plasma. The rate of energy required to sustain this piston wave was calculated to be approximately 10^24 erg/s, which is significantly lower than the energy available from the associated CME. The piston wave's characteristics were compared to those of a previously studied event, revealing similarities in structure and dynamics. The study suggests that the piston wave was driven by a piston-like mechanism rather than a shock wave, and that the energy released by the associated CME was sufficient to power this mechanism.

In the general two Higgs doublet model, the likelihood analysis is performed to study the deviations from the Standard Model in the $W$ boson mass, the muon anomalous magnetic moment, and several flavor processes. The model's parameters are constrained using the Higgs data and a proposed $W$ boson mass measurement. The model's predictions for the $W$ boson mass and the Yukawa coupling ratios are then compared to the current experimental results for $B^0-\bar{B}^0$ mixing, lepton flavour universality anomalies in $B$ decays, and the muon's magnetic moment anomaly. The model's predictions for the $W$ boson mass and the Yukawa coupling ratios are found to be consistent with the current experimental results for a wide range of parameters, and the model's predictions for $W$ mass and Yukawa coupling ratios are found to be consistent with the current experimental results for a wide range of parameters, and the model's predictions for $W$ mass and Yukawa coupling ratios are found to be consistent with the current experimental results for a wide range of parameters.

To account for the effects of fluid turbulence, we've developed a new approach to model the stochastic movement of vortices in two-dimensional incompressible fluids. Our method relies on a precise mathematical equation that accurately captures the fluid's stochastic behavior. We've proven that this equation has a unique solution and that it accurately simulates the fluid's Gaussian vortex dynamics. Our approach enables the use of an efficient numerical method that combines the fluid's deterministic and stochastic components, thus ensuring accurate simulation of vortices in turbulent flows.

We investigate how entanglement behaves in the complex many-body systems of boson sampling. Using the circuit rank of reduced density matrices, we find that the complex linear independence of single-photon states determines the minimum level of entanglement present in the sampled states. Our findings indicate that non-Gaussian states can exhibit similar entanglement properties to Gaussian states, contradicting previous assumptions.

Incorporating the dimension of time in learning from sequences is a major challenge in machine learning, particularly when dealing with high-dimensional data and limited samples. This problem is prevalent in various life science measurements, such as analyzing the behavior of neurons, tracking the movement of particles, and monitoring the behavior of animals. To address this challenge, a novel approach is proposed, which involves using a recurrent neural network to create a compact, low-dimensional representation of temporal sequences. This method allows for the efficient learning of complex patterns and relationships within high-dimensional data streams.

Recurrent neural networks excel in handling tasks with incomplete information, 
yet the connection between their internal states and external observations remains
unclear. This research demonstrates that a particular recurrent network design, 
known as the LSTMs, can effectively model a specific class of partially observable 
environments, known as the finite state machines. By doing so, it is shown that 
LSTMs can internally represent the necessary information about external states, 
independent of the actual number of states involved. This finding also implies 
that RNNs can be seen as a method for creating beliefs about external realities, 
despite the limitations of their memory.

In weakly-supervised action detection, the primary goal is to pinpoint actions within long videos given pre-defined categories and known action occurrences. Current techniques, however, heavily depend on manually crafted features and traditional methods that struggle to capture complex spatial-temporal patterns in data. Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) have been shown to effectively learn intricate patterns in graph-structured data, but their application in video-based action detection has been limited. This paper proposes the first deep learning-based approach to spot detection, incorporating GCNs into the detection process. Our proposed method, referred to as SGCN, leverages GCNs to learn context-aware relationships between actions and their surroundings, thereby enhancing action detection accuracy. Our experiments demonstrate that SGCN outperforms state-of-the-art methods in accuracy, underscoring the value of context learning in action detection.

The 2021 Image Similarity Challenge (2021 ISC) aimed to advance the state-of-the-art in image similarity assessment, a critical task in computer vision.  Following the challenges set by the 2019 and 2020 ISC, the 2021 edition focused on complex, real-world images featuring diverse objects, intricate patterns, and images requiring multi-step reasoning.  A total of 1,024 unique, high-resolution images were used, with 1,024,000 image pairs, 60% of which were positive.  Twenty-four teams participated in the competition, submitting 144 models and 120 submissions.  Notably, the winning team, 2DMatch, developed a two-branch architecture combining CNN and ViT, while the second-place team, UniSim, proposed a unified architecture for both image and text similarity.  Through comprehensive analysis, the challenges and limitations of current methods were identified, paving the way for future advancements.

This work examines a family of one-dimensional parabolic partial differential equations, which model a specific type of stochastic process that incorporates random jumps and has a narrowing boundary on the right side. We are interested in the behavior of these equations when their coefficients undergo small changes, which may occur at different scales. This research extends previous findings on perturbations in one-dimensional diffusion processes to parabolic equations, including cases with a narrowing boundary. It also provides a new perspective on metastable behaviors in such equations, as well as a method for homogenizing parabolic equations with rapidly changing coefficients, including with a narrowing boundary.

The impact of extremely strong magnetic fields on the properties of nuclear matter is explored through the lens of the local density approximation of the variational method. Utilizing the local variational approach, properties of nuclear matter in the presence of such magnetic fields are examined. The application of the local variational approach to this context is justified by its compatibility with the broken symmetry inherent in extremely strong magnetic fields. The LOCV method is employed to calculate the ground state energy of the system, which is then analyzed in terms of its dependence on the magnetic field's strength. The results obtained from this investigation are compared with existing theoretical and experimental findings.

A significant challenge in Federated Learning is balancing secure communication between clients and the server, particularly when clients' data is highly sensitive. To address this issue, we present a novel framework called Differential Privacy-based Secure Communication-efficient Recurrent Encoder (DP-REC), which combines differential privacy and recurrent neural networks to minimize communication overhead. By employing an efficient recurrent encoder, our approach ensures that the model converges to a compact solution, thus reducing the amount of data transmitted. Furthermore, our framework's effectiveness is demonstrated through experiments on real-world datasets, showcasing its ability to provide robust security and significantly reduce communication costs.

A study of far-ultraviolet observations of the Taurus-Perseus-Aquila complex has been conducted, focusing on the cloud's structure and star formation activity. The research, involving a 1980-1981 scan of the region, revealed the presence of FU Orionis objects and young stars, as well as UV-emitting regions associated with star-forming areas. The observed data showed FU Ori to be a prominent source of UV radiation, as well as several other young stars, including TWA 1, TWA 2, and TW Hya. The research also identified UV-emitting regions associated with star-forming areas in FU Ori and other regions, as well as the presence of young stars in these areas. The research further found that the majority of the observed UV-emitting regions were associated with star-forming areas, as well as the presence of young stars in these areas. Table extraction from PDFs is a crucial step in many document analysis tasks, and recent advancements in deep learning have led to the development of neural networks that can identify and extract tables from such documents. However, existing methods struggle with retrieving tables from PDFs due to their structural complexity and the variability in formatting. To address this issue, we propose a novel approach that leverages graph neural networks to represent the structure of tables and their visual attributes, and then uses a novel attention-based mechanism to retrieve tables from PDFs based on their structural and visual characteristics. Our method achieves superior performance compared to existing state-of-the-art techniques on multiple datasets, including the IC-DARwIn dataset, and demonstrates robustness against variations in table formatting and content.

This research investigates the cognitive hierarchies concept in multi-stage games with incomplete information, revealing that there is essentially one non-empty set of equilibria, regardless of the level of reasoning. It is demonstrated that any solution within this set is attainable by level-k reasoning for some level L, which is determined solely by the game's structure, not by individual players' reasoning abilities. Furthermore, this finding is extended to apply to single-stage games with insufficient information.

In Mozambique, the autonomous population estimation system is being developed to support the interim period between the latest and upcoming national censuses. This novel system leverages data from Mozambique's mobile phone industry to provide a more accurate population estimate. By analyzing historical data, the system identifies and replicates the population growth patterns observed in each of the country's provinces and districts. The results demonstrate that the system can provide precise population estimates, with the level of accuracy varying depending on the size of the area being analyzed.

To address the approximate membership query problem, we introduce a novel data structure called the Bloom Filter, which surpasses traditional hash tables by offering constant time complexity for insertions, deletions, and searches, and efficient use of memory. Our analysis also shows that combining bloom filters with hash tables can create a structure that only displays the average-case properties of hash tables, effectively eliminating the potential for worst-case scenarios.

We have developed a theoretical framework for reconfiguring the spin structure of atoms and molecules produced through laser-induced three-body recombination. By applying specific laser configurations, we can transform a spin-coherent spinor component into various spin-coherent molecular components. This process enables the creation of dual-component molecular states with opposing spin structures. Our findings offer a pathway to investigate the distinct interactions between different molecular spin states.

A novel multi-resolution framework for the Smoothed Particle Hydrodynamics method is introduced, enabling the interaction between fluids and solid structures with varying resolutions. This approach allows for a finer particle distribution within areas of interest, thereby enhancing simulation accuracy where it's most needed. By employing a specialized kernel function, a seamless connection is established between simulations conducted at different resolutions, ultimately enabling more efficient and accurate multi-component fluid-structure interaction simulations.

A novel quantum machine learning framework is presented, comprising two key components: a quantum autoencoder and a quantum kernel machine. This framework's adaptation of the autoencoder allows it to be utilized for a range of tasks, from identifying patterns in data to dimensionality reduction. Furthermore, introducing a quantum guidance step enables it to be employed for a more supervised form of dimensionality reduction. When paired with a kernel machine, this framework can be used for a range of supervised tasks, from classification to regression. A major advantage of this framework is its scalability, allowing it to be used on near-term quantum devices with limited qubits. Experimentation on superconducting processors has demonstrated the framework's effectiveness, showcasing its ability to tackle real-world problems, including the analysis of chemical data and a binary classification task.

A recently developed neural TTS model, FastPitch, has enhanced controllability over pitch by incorporating a durational and pitch embedding layer. Nonetheless, the pitch embeddings are randomly generated, which can lead to unwanted acoustic effects. In this paper, we present an innovative approach to generate pitch embeddings based on acoustic pitch information, which maintains the original acoustic characteristics of fastpitch while boosting its pitch control. The proposed method involves retraining FastPitch with generated data, which combines random and calculated embeddings. The results show that our approach yields a 20% improvement in melodic consistency and a 20% improvement in pitch control, while maintaining a 10% degradation in naturalness.

The widespread adoption of IoT devices has led to a significant increase in the volume of data generated over time and across space. This phenomenon is commonly observed in applications such as smart cities, where sensors continuously collect and transmit data. However, existing methods struggle to effectively analyze this data due to the difficulty in identifying patterns within the complex relationships between different data points. This paper addresses the challenge by proposing a deep learning model called Hopper, which is capable of predicting the volume of data generated over time and across space in multi-hop scenarios. The model's design draws inspiration from the hopper insect's ability to navigate and adapt to its environment, and it utilizes a Transformer-based architecture to achieve high accuracy in its predictions. The model's performance is evaluated using real-world datasets, and the results demonstrate its superior capability in predicting the volume of data generated over time and across space in multi-hop scenarios.

The Large Hadron Collider's measurement of how often lepton pairs are created alongside $b\bar{b}$ particle groups is a crucial indicator of the Standard Model of particle physics. Deviations from predicted probabilities can signal the presence of new particles or forces beyond our current understanding. A key challenge in this area is accurately measuring the masses of electrons and positrons, which is complicated by the influence of quantum electrodynamics effects. To address this, a new method has been developed to calculate these corrections, which are then used to refine the mass of the W boson based on LHC data collected at 7 and 8 TeV energies.

This study investigates user experience quality in telepresence robot control by examining the relationship between cognitive load and the quality of experience. An interactive assessment was conducted with 10 users, utilizing the NASA-TLX tool to measure cognitive strain and an in-person evaluation to assess quality of experience. Results indicate a negative correlation between cognitive load and the quality of experience, with specific attention to the significance of interactive elements in shaping user perceptions.

This study introduces the Bayesian hierarchical linear analysis model, a sophisticated statistical tool that integrates Bayesian methods, hierarchical modeling, and linear regression. By incorporating these components, the model enables analysts to address complex data sets with grouped or nested structures, yielding more accurate estimates and predictions. Bayesian methods facilitate the incorporation of prior knowledge and the computation of the full posterior distribution of model parameters. Hierarchical modeling allows for the estimation of population-level distributions and the "borrowing strength" across subgroups. Linear regression provides a versatile framework for modeling the relationship between response and predictor variables. This study presents the Bayesian hierarchical linear analysis model, detailing its core components and applications. Furthermore, the R package 'broom' is employed to demonstrate the practical implementation of the model, specifically in the context of educational data.

This paper builds on the work of Li and Zhang (2019) by creating a comprehensive mathematical framework for the Mafia game, clarifying its underlying principles and setting up key equations. Kibler and Li (2986) introduced a model for the Mafia game's basic dynamics, incorporating the roles of Mafia and townspeople, with corresponding probabilities for their actions. This paper expands on their model by developing a general framework for the Mafia game, incorporating four distinct player types - Mafia, spy, detective, and citizen - with associated probabilities for their actions. To account for the uncertainty of player types, a system of equations is established, with solutions providing the probability of each player being a Mafia or a townspeople. Furthermore, this paper presents two distinct game scenarios - one where all Mafia are aware of each other's identities, and another where they are not - with respective equation systems and solutions.

The formation of a solar system with multiple giant planets is a complex process that is still not fully understood. To investigate how these planets form, we simulated the formation of a pair of massive planets in a protoplanetary disk, considering their growth and the movement of smaller particles within the disk. Our study reveals that when these planets grow simultaneously, they can develop a unique structure in the surrounding disk, characterized by a ring of smaller particles. This process is influenced by the movement of gas and the movement of smaller particles within the disk. Our study also shows that when these planets grow simultaneously, they can develop a larger mass than when they grow one after the other. This process is influenced by the movement of gas and the movement of smaller particles within the disk. Our study provides new insights into the formation of a solar system with multiple giant planets.

The electronic properties of graphene and single-wall carbon nanotubes are characterized by a well-defined Dirac cone structure, whereas their solid-state counterparts exhibit band structures influenced by intertube interactions. Utilizing angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy, our research reveals the presence of a low-energy band structure in a high-quality armchair carbon nanotube film, which deviates from expected free-electron-like dispersion. Notably, we observed a phonon-assisted band structure, which can be attributed to the interaction between tubes, thereby providing insight into the electronic properties of carbon nanotube films.

This paper presents a novel fuzzy k-means clustering approach, called variable feature weighted fuzzy k-means (VFWFKM), that assigns variable weights to data features. Unlike traditional k-means and its fuzzy variants, VFWFKM can handle high-dimensional data more effectively by accounting for feature importance. Our algorithm, built upon the concept of non-negative matrix factorization, iteratively optimizes feature weights and cluster memberships. Experimental results demonstrate that VFWFKM outperforms existing methods in terms of accuracy and efficiency on real-world datasets.

The mixture-of-experts (MoE) model has been a key component in numerous machine learning applications, yet a major challenge persists in determining the optimal parameters for MoE networks, even in the simplest setup involving two experts and one parameter for gating. This difficulty arises because the parameter space contains an infinite number of singular points and an overwhelming number of local minima, rendering standard optimization methods ineffective. This paper presents a solution to this problem by proposing a mixture-of-conditional-experts (MoCE) reparameterization, which circumvents the parameter space's complexities and guarantees a unique representation of MoE models, thus enabling convergence to optimal solutions with standard optimization methods. Specifically, the authors establish a theoretical framework for MoCE and show its equivalence to MoE models, while also demonstrating its efficiency in training through empirical evaluations on image classification and language modeling tasks.

We're exploring the relationship between the Jacobian of a hyperelliptic curve and the set of all possible chip-firing games on it, focusing on the patterns that emerge from these games. Our investigation reveals that the patterns formed by these patterns exhibit a unique symmetry known as hyperelliptic involution symmetry. Furthermore, we're calculating a specific mathematical structure associated with these patterns and finding that it aligns with an established theory involving the decomposition of the Jacobian into simpler components. Our results also show that the patterns formed by these games on a specific subset of the curve are equivalent to the original pattern, thus confirming that the pattern's unique identity remains unchanged.

The existence of global symmetries in quantum gravity is not supported, according to some theories. This lack of support could be attributed to various mechanisms, such as black holes, which might break these symmetries and release them in the form of U(1) gauge symmetries. These mechanisms could leave observable traces, such as large-scale polarization patterns in the cosmic background radiation. We examine the potential impact of breaking global symmetries on the production of gravitational waves and other cosmological phenomena. We find that global symmetry breaking could lead to the formation of cosmic strings and other topological defects, which could be detected through their gravitational wave signatures. We also explore the potential impact of these mechanisms on the formation of large-scale structures in the universe.

The use of UVIT on the VLT has allowed for the creation of the most detailed UV images of the Virgo cluster NGC 4147 to date. By analyzing the data, we found that the cluster exhibits a UV excess, particularly in its core, and that the brightest stars in the UV spectrum are concentrated there. Our study of the cluster's color-magnitude diagram revealed the presence of blue horizontal branch stars, and that the cluster's blue tail extends to the turn-off point. Additionally, we found that the cluster contains a significant number of blue straggler stars, and that the distribution of these stars is consistent with that of other Virgo cluster members.

This note provides a proof of the Mumford Conjecture in the context of the moduli space for smooth projective varieties with fixed genus, specifically utilizing the t-structure from the weight filtration in the theory of mixed Hodge theory.

The notion of model transferability has been widely accepted in deep learning, with two key principles underlying it. The first principle suggests that pre-trained models transfer knowledge effectively when trained on large datasets, and applied to related tasks on comparable scales. The second principle proposes that pre-trained models excel on visually similar tasks, regardless of dataset size. However, contrary to these assumptions, our research reveals that these principles are overly simplistic and often inaccurate. Through a comprehensive evaluation of state-of-the-art models, we found that dataset characteristics, such as the number of classes and image count, are more influential in transfer learning than previously thought. Furthermore, our results show that source and target domains do not need to be visually similar for effective transfer learning. These findings have significant implications for the transfer learning process and highlight the need for more nuanced approaches to understanding model transferability.

Information spread within interconnected networks is a common occurrence, yet its speed is heavily influenced by the network's structural characteristics. To better understand this relationship, researchers have developed a model that simulates information diffusion across networks of varying complexity. By analyzing the results, they found that strongly connected individuals act as crucial intermediaries, accelerating information transfer. Furthermore, they discovered that the model's outcomes align with a universal principle, stating that information diffusion speed is directly related to the network's modular structure. This principle holds true across different network types, including those with random and directed connections.

We establish a specific form of the distinctiveness conjecture put forth by Thomas and Yau. Our investigation focuses on capillary surfaces that have a certain area constraint and reside within the half space. A key finding of our research is that mean curvature has a definite, non-zero, minimum value, which in turn enables us to create a precise, quantifiable measure of topological distinctiveness for these surfaces. This outcome is a direct result of a new, proven estimate for the first eigenvalue of the Laplacian in a capillary droplet with a given adhesion angle. Our research also provides an upper limit for this eigenvalue in the context of the first eigenfunction.

The model's accuracy is evaluated using a perturbation analysis in discrete time, focusing on a standard model for regular perturbation in unamplified sections. A key factor in this analysis is the number of digital conversions per symbol, which is influenced by the time it takes for a signal to traverse a fiber link. This study derives a formula for this key factor and verifies its effectiveness through numerical testing.

Android has become the most widely used operating system, accounting for over 70% of the global smartphone market. Its open-source nature has made it a prime target for security researchers, who have identified various vulnerabilities in the Android ecosystem. One such vulnerability is Issue-Space Evasion (ISE) attacks, which exploit Android's open-source nature to bypass security measures. This paper provides a comprehensive review of ISE attacks, discussing their mechanisms, impacts, and potential countermeasures. The authors also highlight the need for further research in this area to better understand and mitigate ISE attacks.

Distributed systems have become a cornerstone of modern distributed computing, with numerous applications such as data processing, storage, and communication. However, designing such systems is a complex task, requiring developers to navigate intricate infrastructure, manage intricate dependencies, and contend with various failure scenarios. To address these challenges, Ozy, a universal orchestration container, is introduced to streamline the development of distributed systems. By encapsulating the underlying infrastructure, dependencies, and failure handling, it enables the creation of distributed systems with minimal code, allowing for the rapid integration of new services and the incorporation of new features.

The reentrant quantum Hall phase, which occurs in thin semiconductor films, is characterized by the disappearance and reappearance of the half-integer quantum Hall effect as the magnetic field increases. The phenomenon has been extensively studied for various interaction strengths and filling factors, but our research reveals a previously unobserved reentrant phase for the filling factor of 5/2 under moderate levels of Landau level mixing. This discovery is significant as it may facilitate the experimental observation of the topological 5/2 quantum Hall state.

Investigating the properties of gravitationally bound systems in an expanding universe is a complex task, and one approach involves analyzing the Thakurta metric, which describes the Thakurta black hole. This approach, however, has its limitations, and we demonstrate that the Thakurta black hole does not accurately represent a solitary cosmological black hole. Consequently, we establish an upper limit on the abundance of primordial black holes that could have served as the precursors to the gravitational waves detected by LIGO-Virgo, and we reiterate that these results are not affected by the Thakurta black hole's shortcomings.

The rapid formation of planetary cores through the accumulation of dust particles is a plausible explanation for core mass limitations and gas giant origins. The efficiency of this process relies on particle behavior within a disk, which is influenced by a parameter called the particle Stokes number. The conventional approach assumes a uniform distribution of particles, but the formation of localized particle clusters may occur due to a phenomenon known as clustering. The current study examines the impact of clustering on planet formation by incorporating a model that simulates particle movement within a disk. The results show that clustering significantly affects planet formation, with lower Stokes numbers leading to faster formation times and higher masses of solid particles in the inner disk regions. The research also reveals that variations in Stokes number can lead to significant differences in planet formation times and masses, with lower Stokes numbers resulting in more efficient formation. The study's findings suggest that the conventional approach may underestimate the efficiency of planet formation and that the impact of clustering should be considered in planetary formation models.

Overparameterized models can generalize effectively despite having more parameters than necessary to fit the training data. Theoretical explanations for this phenomenon are still limited. This paper demonstrates that models with only a polynomial number of parameters can be forced into overparameterization by computational restrictions, thus providing a more comprehensive explanation for this phenomenon. The study also extends existing hardness results to broader model classes, including those with non-convex optimization and model averaging, as well as a specific class of parities, showing that these models cannot efficiently fit random data under certain computational constraints.

In an infinite, locally compact Hausdorff group, a subset is considered Bohr if it remains unchanged under the group's operation. We previously established that for any finite set in such a group, its sumset and difference set are also Bohr sets. This paper further explores this concept by proving that in a countably infinite group, a non-trivial Bohr set is a neighborhood in the group's Bohr topology. This result is achieved using a method inspired by a theorem of Sierpinski. Additionally, our findings demonstrate that a specific countably infinite group has the property that the preimage of any Bohr set under a group homomorphism is also a Bohr set, and we establish that an enumerable group has this property if and only if it is a quotient of a free abelian group of some cardinality.

This paper tackles the dial-a-ride problem in an urban setting by proposing a Branch-and-Cut algorithm to solve it efficiently. The proposed method focuses on two key objectives: first, it develops an integer programming formulation to model the problem and generate initial strong bounds; second, it develops a large neighbourhood search heuristic to produce high-quality feasible solutions that can be used as upper bounds. The results show that, despite its limitations, a simple greedy heuristic can produce surprisingly good results. However, to model complex constraints, we also introduce a set partitioning formulation that enables us to explore a larger solution space. The combination of these approaches allows the algorithm to solve instances with up to 50 customers to optimality within a reasonable timeframe.

This research introduces a groundbreaking approach to integrating knowledge into multi-modal learning systems, specifically within the e-commerce sector. We propose the Knowledge Understood Multi-modal Pretraining (KUMoP) framework, which leverages the power of deep learning models to process diverse data types, including images, text, and knowledge graphs. KUMoP pre-trains these models using a self-supervised learning strategy, allowing them to effectively capture and represent complex relationships between different modalities. We demonstrate the effectiveness of KUMoP through comprehensive experiments on two e-commerce tasks: product search and recommendation, where it achieves superior performance compared to state-of-the-art methods.

A novel deep learning model, the Deep InfoMax (DIM), has been developed for unsupervised learning of deep generative models, particularly in the medical domain. The model's potential for predicting the progression of Alzheimer's disease (AD) has been demonstrated through its application to the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) dataset. The study's results indicate that the learned representations of MRI and PET images can effectively forecast progression to AD at a later time point, with significant implications for early detection and intervention.

A cutting-edge AI system, based on a Language Semantics Comprehension (LSC) model, is essential for developing Natural Language Processing (NLP) applications. Recent studies have examined the capabilities of humans and animals in understanding language semantics, but the knowledge gained from these studies remains largely theoretical. This paper presents a novel LSC model that utilizes a recurrent neural network (RNN) to simulate human language semantics comprehension. The proposed model incorporates two key components: a word embedding layer that generates word vectors and a sequential neural network that processes sequences of these vectors. The sequential network is designed to capture the context of a sentence and produce an output vector that represents the sentence's semantics. This model was evaluated using a large dataset of 10 million Chinese sentences and demonstrated impressive results, achieving an accuracy of 92.3% on a benchmark task. The proposed model's effectiveness was further validated through a series of ablation studies, which showed that it outperforms existing LSC models.

We have found that a correlated metal with local quadrupolar order exhibits a unique property where the interactions between electrons and between electrons and lattice vibrations lead to an increased spin-orbit coupling. This increase is due to the presence of a specific type of interaction that causes the increased spin-orbit coupling, and we have found two materials, strontium and barium hexatelluride, which exhibit this property. This discovery provides new insight into the relationship between electron interactions and spin-orbit coupling, and may have implications for the development of new materials with unique properties.

We suggest a novel approach to explain the nature of dark matter, namely that it is a form of "shadow matter" existing in a separate, metastable universe that shares similar physical properties but differs in its cosmological parameters. This shadow sector, which has no direct connection to the visible sector, is composed of particles that interact solely through gravity. We explore the implications of this idea, particularly in the context of cosmological observations, and discuss potential ways to test the hypothesis experimentally.

The growing presence of AI-powered medical devices in healthcare settings has led to a pressing need for reliable methods to assess their performance under various distribution scenarios. This study proposes a novel approach to estimate the effectiveness of AI medical devices by accounting for distribution shifts, which can occur due to changes in patient demographics or data collection methods. By leveraging the concept of conformal prediction, our method can adapt to different distribution scenarios without requiring prior knowledge of the underlying data distribution. Through simulations and real-world experiments, we demonstrate the efficacy of our approach in accurately evaluating the performance of AI medical devices under various distribution scenarios.

A new method for efficiently exploring the conformational space of biomolecules has been developed, by using the conformational variability of double-stranded DNA as a proof of concept. This approach leverages the advantages of molecular dynamics simulations, where a substrate holds one strand of the DNA sequence in a fixed position, enabling the free movement of the other strand. This substrate-based biasing technique is particularly useful for identifying the underlying factors that influence DNA conformation, as well as for uncovering the conformations that are rarely observed in natural conditions. The method has been successfully applied to a series of double-stranded DNA sequences, where a substrate holding the 5' strand of each sequence enabled the formation of diverse structures, including hairpins, stacked dimers, and parallel and antiparallel duplexes. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of substrate-based biasing in identifying the underlying factors that control DNA conformation, as well as in uncovering the conformations that are rarely observed in natural conditions.

The Adaptive Numbering System (ANS) is a highly efficient entropy encoding technique, widely regarded as the gold standard in modern entropy encoding. Despite its exceptional performance, a thorough understanding of its underlying mechanics remains limited. This study delves into the intricacies of the ANS, examining its internal workings and evaluating its effectiveness in the context of lossless data compression. By unraveling the complexities of the ANS, we aim to shed light on its encoding and decoding processes and uncover its potential for further optimization.

The dielectric properties of pore solutions in cement-based materials are investigated using the finite-element method. The study focuses on how the dielectric constant and loss factor are influenced by the temperature, pore solution composition, and pore structure. The results show that the dielectric constant and loss factor are significantly affected by the temperature and ion concentration within the pore solution, and that structural variations in the material can lead to differences in the dielectric properties. The findings are compared with experimental data and dielectric spectroscopy measurements, and the study highlights the importance of considering the dielectric properties of pore solutions in the development of cement-based materials.

In this study, a thorough examination of heavy-hadron molecules is conducted, encompassing both low-mass and high-mass variants. A particular focus is placed on the mass range of 2-3 GeV, where a diverse array of candidate particles exists. The underlying theoretical framework for molecule formation is critically evaluated, with the strong interaction being the primary driving force. The study delves into the characteristics of the hadronic molecules, including their masses, decay patterns, and the distinct properties that set them apart from their compact counterparts. The findings are compared with experimental data, and the prospects for identifying heavy-hadronic molecules are discussed.

Die Untersuchung der Entwicklungstendenzen von militärischen, schwarmartigen unbemannten Systemen mittels natural language processing wird durch die rasante Zunahme von wissenschaftlichen Publikationen in den letzten Jahren erschwert. Diese Herausforderung wird durch die unzureichende Verfügbarkeit von automatisierten Analyseverfahren für wissenschaftliche Texte noch verstärkt. In diesem Kontext untersucht die vorliegende Arbeit die potenziellen Entwicklungstreiber und die zukünftige Ausrichtung von Projekten im Bereich der militärischen, schwarmartigen unbemannten Systeme. Als Lösung für dieses Problem wird ein neuer Ansatz zur Extraktion von Informationen aus den Texten entwickelt, der es ermöglicht, die Entwicklungstendenzen von Projekten zu analysieren und die zukünftige Ausrichtung von Forschung und Entwicklung in diesem Bereich zu identifizieren.
