This article outlines a comprehensive approach to leveraging LLMs and search engines in conjunction to create a search-based system that effectively answers questions. We discuss the essential components of this system, including the selection of an LLM, the DPR retriever, and the query generation process, before delving into the details of fine-tuning these components for improved search-based question-answering.

This study derives a solution to a longstanding problem posed by Billingsley regarding the long-term behavior of linear functional $L$ defined on the space of polynomials. The functional's value on a polynomial $p$ is determined by the integral of $p(x)$ with a weight function $w(x)$ that includes a logarithmic term, specifically $\frac{1}{\ln|x-a|}$. The study also provides a method for calculating the functional's associated polynomials and confirms that these polynomials can be expressed using Jacobi polynomials. The solution is achieved by expressing a system of linear equations in terms of Chebyshev polynomials and solving it using the method of generating functions. The study employs a modified version of the method of generating functions to calculate the coefficients of the generating function. The study's results are further supported by numerical examples.

A persistent issue with crowdsourcing platforms like Amazon Mechanical Turk (MTurk) is the challenge of identifying skilled workers. To address this, we present a new approach, the Qualification Search Algorithm (QuSA), which identifies workers based on their past performance in relevant tasks. Our study demonstrates the effectiveness of QuSA in selecting workers for complex tasks, such as identifying anomalies in images, outperforming existing methods and standard search methods.

Text-video retrieval, a crucial component of video search, can be effectively achieved through two primary approaches: matching video frames to text descriptions or matching videos to extracted tokens. While transformer-based methods excel at matching tokens, they often overlook the spatial relationships between visual features and text words. To address this limitation, we propose TS2-Net, a transformer model that incorporates spatial information and utilizes a shifting mechanism to align spatially correlated tokens. The TS2-Net architecture combines shifty and selectional transformers to capture dynamic spatial relationships between text and frame tokens, while also learning a unified representation space. Experimental results demonstrate that TS2-Net outperforms existing approaches on MSRVTT, VATEX, and LSMDC datasets, showcasing its effectiveness in text-video matching.

We investigate a new flavor-changing neutral current process, specifically $t\rightarrow I\gamma$ where $I$ denotes the invisible particle state. Our analysis reveals that within the $\Lambda$-MSSM framework, the $t\rightarrow I\gamma$ decay is dominated by the direct coupling between the top and Higgsino states. This interaction is facilitated by a coupling term, $\lambda_{311}$, which allows for a significant increase in the invisible decay rate of the top quark. Our research indicates that the invisible decay rate can reach up to $10^{-4}$ times the standard model prediction for $\gamma\gamma$ processes. This finding has significant implications for top quark decay studies and may provide valuable insights into supersymmetry and beyond standard model physics.

We've developed a Hybrid Random Graph (HRG) model that combines the Preferential Attachment (PA) and Uniform Attachment (UA) rules. In this network, edges are formed by randomly selecting vertices, and if PA is used, the likelihood of a vertex being chosen is proportional to its degree. Conversely, if UA is used, the likelihood is proportional to the vertex's index. We've derived an algorithm to simulate directed HRGs and derived mathematical expressions for the degree distribution of these networks. We've also demonstrated that directed HRGs exhibit a power-law distribution of out-degrees when Preferential Attachment is used and all other parameters remain constant. Furthermore, we've shown that when Uniform Attachment is used, the network exhibits a power-law distribution of in-degrees. We've also derived the distribution of edge-weighted path lengths and found that it follows an exponential distribution. We've also analyzed the network clustering coefficient and found that it converges to a constant value. We've also studied the network connectivity and found that it converges to a constant value. We've also analyzed the network connectivity and found that it converges to a constant value.

A significant challenge in modern neural network research is identifying multiple disturbances simultaneously in wireless networks. This issue is particularly pronounced in deep learning models, which struggle to accurately classify complex patterns. To address this limitation, a new approach called MLWID-CNN has been developed. This innovative model employs a multi-channel convolutional neural network to recognize disturbances in wireless signals. By utilizing a data augmentation technique, MLWID-CNN can effectively learn and identify patterns in these signals. Furthermore, the model's architecture allows for accurate classification of multiple disturbances simultaneously. To validate the model's capabilities, a comprehensive dataset called MLWID-Data has been created. This dataset includes a wide range of wireless signal patterns and can be used to train and test the model's performance. Experimental results demonstrate that MLWID-CNN achieves a high accuracy rate of 98.4% in identifying disturbances in wireless signals.

Building upon Som-Raychaudhuri's work, we investigated the effects of electric charges on Klein-Gordon particles in the presence of a cosmic string with a dislocation. We derived the Klein-Gordon equation for this scenario and employed the Nikiforov-Yumev method to obtain an exact solution. We then explored the impact of the string parameter, dislocation, electric charge, and energy-dependent energy on the particles' behavior. Notably, we found that the parameters influencing geometry also affect the particles, while the parameters representing energy and charge influence the particles' behavior in a manner analogous to gravitational effects.

A measure algebra is considered usual if it can be represented as a subalgebra of the continuous functions with compact support on a locally compact Hausdorff space, where the measure corresponds to the integration against a specific probability measure. This paper demonstrates that every locally compact group with Haar measure, every probability space, and every measure space possess a usual measure algebra.

Measuring the longitudinal spin asymmetry in the deeply virtual Compton scattering process with a transversely polarized beam allows us to distinguish it from other processes and provides insights into the gluon GPDs. This measurement is particularly feasible at the Electron-Ion Collider, where the high-energy beam can effectively distinguish the scattering and the Compton processes. Our study focuses on analyzing the recoil proton's polarization in the deeply virtual Compton scattering process at the EIC, where we found that the polarization serves as a distinguishing observable. This measurement can help us differentiate the deeply virtual Compton scattering process from the deeply virtual Compton scattering process with a virtual exchange. This new observable provides an additional tool for extracting the deeply virtual Compton scattering amplitude in the deeply virtual Compton scattering process.

As the capabilities of synthetic minds have expanded, they have become increasingly integrated into our everyday lives, prompting a need for a comprehensive framework to guide their development. This paper proposes a conceptual framework for augmenting artificial intelligence to create more human-like minds. It outlines the key components of this framework and discusses its significance in understanding the synthetic mind, while also considering potential applications and implications.

Bosons with spin-orbit connections in optical lattices can exhibit modulated superfluid phases, characterized by a long superfluid phase transition and a first-order normal-insulator phase transition. Utilizing a mean-field approach, we investigate how temperature impacts these transitions. Our results show that increasing temperature causes the long superfluid phase transition to shift towards lower critical points and temperatures, while also reducing the critical temperature of the normal-insulator phase. Furthermore, we find that the first-order transition evolves into a second-order phase transition at a specific temperature, where the critical point's location is temperature-dependent.

Given a finite abelian group $G$, we consider the graph $\mathcal{G}(G)$ where the vertices are the elements of $G$ and an edge exists between two vertices if their difference is a unit in $G$. This study focuses on the graph $\mathcal{G}(G)$ for specific groups, including $\mathbb{Z}_n$, $\mathbb{Z}_n^2$, $\mathbb{Z}_n^3$, and $\mathbb{Z}_4^2$, and examines the effects of merging certain elements on the graph's properties. Merging elements with even or odd characteristics in these groups results in distinct types of degenerations, and these effects are explored in detail.

This research explores the properties of AdS$_3$/CFT$_2$ and AdS$_2$/CFT$_1$ dualities, specifically those linked to two-dimensional superconformal field theories. We concentrate on theories that are mass-deformed, as generated by the Schiappa-Kraus-Witten background of massive Type IIA string theory. The investigation involves examining the low-energy dynamics of D6-branes in this background, as well as the renormalization group flow of the corresponding superconformal field theories. The results reveal the emergence of AdS$_3$/CFT$_2$ and AdS$_2$/CFT$_1$ dualities, which can be understood through the behavior of the low-energy states. The findings also show that the AdS$_3$/CFT$_2$ and AdS$_2$/CFT$_1$ central charges are directly related to the five-brane and D0-charge wrappings, respectively. The research further demonstrates that the Schiappa-Kraus-Witten background contains a complete set of mass deformations, which can be used to construct a comprehensive map of the theoretical landscape.

We're developing novel kernels for Gaussian Process regression based on straightforward mathematical concepts. These new kernels can be broken down into simpler parts, making them suitable for complex, multi-dimensional spaces. We're comparing these kernels with more conventional alternatives in terms of accuracy and computational efficiency.

Achieving the goal of a $500\,\mathrm{GeV}$ muon collider is hindered by beam-induced noise, which poses a significant challenge to achieving the necessary luminosity. To address this issue, we examine various strategies to mitigate noise, including enhancing the visibility of hadronic particles through advanced detector design and innovative reconstruction techniques. Our analysis encompasses a wide range of beam parameters and different beam hosing patterns, as well as exploring the potential of using advanced tracking detectors to improve visibility. Ultimately, we demonstrate that combining advanced tracking technology with novel reconstruction methods can significantly reduce beam-induced noise, thereby making the goal of a $500\,\mathrm{GeV}$ muon collider more attainable.

We introduce Spartan, a novel class of differentiable sparsity-inducing methods that encompass both $l_0$ and $l_1$ regularizations. By leveraging an optimal transportation theory-based formulation, these sparsity methods can be seamlessly integrated into gradient-based optimization frameworks. Our theory demonstrates the existence of a unique, differentiable, and non-trivial optimal transportation plan for every non-zero cost matrix. Moreover, the gradient of this plan exhibits continuous and differentiable properties with respect to the matrix's elements. Our experiments demonstrate that Spartan offers superior performance compared to the traditional $l_0$ and $l_1$ regularizations across various tasks, including image classification, natural language processing, and reinforcement learning.

A unique phenomenon arises in systems of bosons where their behavior is restricted by the exclusion principle, typically associated with fermions. In our research, we've discovered this phenomenon in a weakly interacting Bose gas confined to two dimensions and at low temperatures. The formation of a vortex when the container is rotated demonstrates a clear manifestation of Pauli blocking, effectively preventing the creation of vortices below a specific rotation speed. The observed blocking effect is a direct result of the three-dimensional nature of the system, and our study reveals that it persists even when the size of the container is much larger than the associated wavelength.

A widely accepted notion among researchers is that code smell detection tools are beneficial for developers, but this idea is not supported by empirical evidence. Our study aimed to fill this gap by examining software developers' perspectives on the impact of test smells, which are a specific type of code smell. Through a survey of 100 software developers, we discovered that these professionals consider test smells to be more detrimental than other code smells, with the most significant negative effects being the reduction in code readability and the increased likelihood of defects. Our findings suggest that developers value test quality and clarity above all else, and that the severity of test smells is more pronounced than that of code smells in general.

We develop a novel statistical testing method, breaking the constraints of existing
multivariate outlier detection techniques that are limited to one-dimensional or
low-dimensional datasets. Our approach is grounded in the brushing process, a non-convex
integro-differential equation, which can be applied to high-dimensional data.
We derive conditions under which the brushing process is both well-defined and stable,
and we prove that it is capable of accurately identifying outliers in a wide range
of data distributions. Our results are supported by extensive numerical experiments.

The KKMCee event generator, a well-established tool for simulating $\gamma\gamma$ collisions, has been enhanced with the ability to model quark pair creation in addition to lepton pairs. This upgrade is crucial for the design of future high-energy lepton colliders, where significant background noise from hadrons produced by $\gamma\gamma$ collisions will need to be accounted for in detector development and data analysis. Furthermore, the upgraded generator will be instrumental in analyzing data from the LHeC and a future $\eph$ collider.

Inter-Beat Interval (IBI) signals, recorded by wearable devices, are prone to noise and gaps, making them difficult to analyze. Accurate IBI analysis is crucial for understanding heart rate variability, which is a valuable indicator of cardiac health. In this research, a novel method is introduced to estimate IBI signals, utilizing the Tiramisu model for signal inpainting. This method outperforms existing approaches in terms of precision and efficiency, as evidenced by high correlation coefficients and low root mean square error in simulation tests. The proposed method's success is attributed to its ability to fill in missing IBI signal components, resulting in a more accurate and reliable IBI estimation.

Low-rank tensor approximation techniques, particularly the Tucker model, have been widely applied in data analysis. Recent research has introduced randomized algorithms for efficient tensor decomposition, focusing on the underexplored scenario where multiple passes over the data are allowed. Our study reveals that an existing randomized method can be simplified for this scenario, and we propose a more efficient alternative. We also provide theoretical bounds for the accuracy of these algorithms, and through experiments, demonstrate their effectiveness in approximating Tucker tensors.

Graphs are widely used to represent complex data in various fields, and graph embedding is a crucial technique that translates these graphs into low-dimensional vector forms. However, most existing methods are designed for static graphs and fail to capture the dynamic nature of real-world graphs that change over time. This paper reviews and discusses recent advancements in graph embedding techniques that can handle the temporal evolution of graphs, highlighting their applications, challenges, and potential future research directions.

The $^7$H nucleus, consisting of three neutrons and four protons, is hypothesized to be the most neutron-rich hydrogen isotope. However, its existence remains uncertain due to the stability of the $^5$He resonance. As a result, $^7$H cannot be considered a ground state. Instead, it is proposed that $^7$H exists as an excited state formed by the combination of $^3$H and four unbound neutrons. This theory is supported by data from the TRIUMF experiment, which measured the energy released during the reaction of $^6$H and neutrons to produce $^7$H. The findings indicate that $^7$H exists as a short-lived, excited state with an energy of 1.5 MeV above the $^3$H and four neutrons threshold. This has significant implications for understanding the nuclear reactions that occur in the universe, particularly those that take place in the conditions of a supernova explosion.

This paper focuses on solving the Nirenberg problem on half spheres, where we're given a prescribed function f and our goal is to find a conformal factor u in the metric e^2u times the standard metric on the boundary of the upper half space R^+ such that the scalar curvature is f times the Dirac delta function at the origin. Our main finding indicates that under certain conditions, there are no non-trivial solutions to this problem, where "trivial" refers to the standard conformal form of the upper half space metric.

Deep learning models have become the go-to choice for numerous tasks, but their limitations are often apparent when considering their inability to provide guarantees on sample efficiency and theoretical insights. In contrast, optimal transport theory offers powerful tools for data representation and learning, and can complement traditional neural networks. This paper focuses on using optimal transport as a regularizer in deep learning models, and demonstrates its potential to provide guarantees on convergence and generalization. The authors propose a new optimal transport-based regularizer that can be efficiently computed, and show through experiments that it outperforms existing methods in various scenarios.

In the United Kingdom, local authorities have been tasked with managing COVID-19 contact tracing, a task that has been complicated by varying capabilities among the 37 local tracing partnerships in England. To address this disparity, we analyzed data from all partnerships to determine the impact of their size and resources on the effectiveness of the tracing process. Our analysis revealed that, on average, only 40% of contacts were identified, with significant disparities among the partnerships, ranging from 17% to 66%. Notably, larger partnerships tended to identify a higher percentage of contacts, and we estimate that a 10% increase in the number of traced contacts could lead to a 10-15% decrease in the prevalence of the disease. These findings suggest that the quality of COVID-19 contact tracing in England is inconsistent and may contribute to the spread of the virus.

To determine the properties of the Melotte 72 open cluster, we analyzed the photometric and astrometric data from Gaia DR2.  By defining member stars based on their distance and density, we created a more accurate representation of the cluster's properties.  By correcting the cluster's colors for dust, we were able to construct a precise main sequence and identify the cluster's turn-off point.  By fitting a power law to the cluster's main sequence, we were able to determine its age and distance.  Our results indicate that the cluster's age is approximately 1.0 billion years and its distance is approximately 1.6 kiloparsecs.  By analyzing the cluster's kinematics, we were able to determine its position in the Galaxy's disk and identify its membership.  By comparing the cluster's properties to other clusters, we were able to identify its unique characteristics.

We investigate the distribution of Betti numbers in a specific class of random simplicial complexes, known as Gaussian linear complexes, as their size approaches infinity in a specific direction referred to as the sparse regime. Under these conditions, we establish mean values and variance for the Betti numbers and demonstrate that, with increasing probability, they exhibit distinct asymptotic patterns. Furthermore, we derive precise estimates for the Betti numbers in this regime and show that they adhere to a specific normal distribution as their complex size increases without limit.

Robotic systems with multiple cameras can greatly enhance perception capabilities, 
but they often require precise calibration to produce reliable results. Manual 
calibration can be a time-consuming and complex process, particularly when 
dealing with robotic arms that have multiple degrees of freedom. In this paper, 
we explore the potential for automatically adjusting robotic arms to optimize 
camera alignment, based on the visual coherence of images captured by the system. 
Our proposed method relies on simulated training data and demonstrates its 
efficacy on both robotic and non-robotic image sets, including a real-world 
hand-eye coordination task. By leveraging this approach, robotic systems can be 
readily adapted to new configurations without the need for manual recalibration.

Constrained reinforcement learning focuses on finding the best policy that maximizes rewards while adhering to specific constraints. Reverse constrained reinforcement learning, our new framework, involves finding the most constrained policy that achieves a target reward. We develop a dual problem for reverse RL and provide a dual-feasible solution, which yields a policy that closely adheres to the reward constraint. We demonstrate through experiments that our approach outperforms existing methods in both convergence and accuracy.

The European Space Agency's GAIA mission, launched in 2013, has significantly advanced our understanding of the Milky Way galaxy. By providing an extensive dataset of stellar characteristics, including positions, velocities, and ages, GAIA enables researchers to explore the galaxy's structure, evolution, and future. Researchers are leveraging GAIA's data to create 3D models of the galaxy, uncovering new insights into its composition, structure, and evolution. This article discusses the GAIA project, its data release, and the emerging field of 3D galaxy modeling.

We have devised efficient algorithms for creating $O(\sqrt{k})$-sized vertex splits that reduce the graph's treewidth by a factor of $k$. These algorithms run in $O(n^{2} m)$ time and can be accelerated to $O(n^{2} + m)$ for planar graphs. Our methods build upon the standard linear-time approximation algorithm for graph separators, which achieves a $k/\sqrt{2}$ ratio. To improve upon this, we developed two novel algorithms: a randomized method inspired by $k$-component separators, and a deterministic algorithm inspired by nonlinear approximation techniques. Both algorithms maintain $O(n^{2} m)$ runtime, and the latter can be further optimized to $O(n^{2} + m)$ for planar graphs.

The analysis of networks with both positive and negative connections is crucial in multiple disciplines. Research has shown that the methods for detecting such networks, particularly the Weighted Directed Grouping (WDG) method, can uncover complex relationships between different types of network edges. However, the implications of the WDG method's ability to identify groups based on inferred edge types have not been thoroughly examined. We have investigated the conditions under which the WDG method can accurately identify groups based on the network's underlying structure and have found that the method's performance is influenced by several key factors, including the distribution of network edge types and the size of the networks. We have also proposed an extension of the WDG method that can accommodate networks with a mix of inferred and measured edges.

Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) are a prominent example of integrating domain knowledge into machine learning, allowing for more efficient and accurate model training. However, the versatility of PINNs is hindered by their lack of transparency and the uncertainty surrounding their error rates. To address this issue, we have developed a certified error estimation method for PINNs, providing a posteriori validation of their predictions. Our approach involves defining a verification functional that quantifies the residual error of PINNs, and then using this measure to assess the accuracy of their predictions. To illustrate the efficacy of our method, we have applied it to a system of nonlinear equations describing fluid flow in two dimensions.

In recent years, the increasing availability of data from air quality monitoring stations has led to a significant boost in the number of epidemiologic studies examining the impact of air pollution on human health. The development of advanced algorithms for air quality forecasting and the use of machine learning techniques have further enhanced our understanding of the relationship between exposure to pollutants and disease risk. This article provides an overview of the most recent advancements in the field, with a particular focus on the application of geostatistics and machine learning models to the assessment of air quality and the prediction of disease outcomes.

To differentiate between zero bias peaks resulting from Andreev reflection and other peaks, we suggest performing tunneling spectroscopy with an environment of ohmic dissipation. The setup involves using a traditional superconducting probe in conjunction with an intermediate resistive layer and a normal metal sample. The zero bias peak produced by Majorana modes is the only feature that remains unaffected by dissipation. Our theoretical model is based on the Anderson model of dissipation, and we have developed a numerical method to calculate the tunneling density of states. The results of our calculations show that the dissipation strength is determined by the resistance of the intermediate layer, which is directly related to the resistance of the entire device according to the Anderson model. The calculated spectra are in line with the findings of recent experiments, and we have determined the optimal device parameters to suppress zero bias peaks resulting from non-topological sources.

We examine a linear bandit problem with an expanded set of actions, where we derive a suboptimal algorithm that achieves a regret of $O(dKT\sqrt{\log K})$ under certain conditions. This performance is notably better than the $O(K^{\frac{d+1}{2}}T^{\frac{1}{2}})$ regret in cases where $d$ is significantly larger than $\log T$. This improved performance has significant implications for online learning in scenarios involving a vast action space. We demonstrate this by applying our algorithm to a policy inference challenge in reinforcement learning, where we derive a computationally efficient method for solving the problem, and show through experiments that it outperforms a standard approach.

Graphene's lattice symmetry allows for the existence of both optical and mechanical properties that depend on the direction of the valley, known as the valley Hall effect, in response to external disturbances. Our research reveals another method to achieve this same result, involving the creation of specific distortions within the graphene structure. By warping the graphene, we can induce a specific type of spin that depends on the valley orientation, resulting in the movement of charge in opposite directions for different valley configurations. This discovery allows for the selection of specific valley orientations through either mechanical manipulation or electrical application, and we demonstrate the potential for this effect to be utilized in devices based on graphene.

The effectiveness of graph neural networks (GNNs) relies heavily on the quality of graph data, which can be compromised by intentional data manipulation. To study this vulnerability, we developed a strategy for a malicious agent to corrupt GNN training data using reinforcement learning. Our approach involves a multi-objective reward system that considers both the accuracy of the GNN and the agent's own success rate. We tested this strategy on node classification tasks using the Cora and Citeseer datasets, and found that the agent's ability to evade detection was comparable to its ability to cause damage.

To improve the accuracy of cross-referencing between star catalogs, a novel photometric method is introduced, complementing the existing astrometric approach. The proposed method leverages the differences in magnitudes between stars to create a more comprehensive matching framework. By incorporating astrometric and photometric data, a combined metric is developed, allowing for the precise determination of star match probabilities. The efficacy of this method is demonstrated through its application to catalogue pairings, showcasing its potential to enhance the accuracy of astrometric matching.

We establish that in any infinite k-uniform hypergraph with edges as k-vertex sets, and given a subset of its vertices, one can find a small, constant-size subset of those vertices, such that adding the remaining vertices of the original subset to these chosen vertices always forms an edge. The size of this small subset depends only on the maximum degree of the hypergraph and the uniformity of its edges. This result has significant implications for the study of large subsets in the context of Szemerédi's Regularity Lemma, and we further demonstrate its utility in solving specific problems, such as finding large subsets that satisfy certain combinatorial properties in the case of 3-uniform hypergraphs.

Large knowledge bases, such as ontologies, facilitate seamless data exchange across disparate systems, enabling smooth interoperability. However, traditional knowledge graphs rely on predefined categories, limiting their scalability and adaptability. To address this gap, OntoPlot, an innovative visualization tool, has been developed to effectively display complex, non-hierarchical relationships within extensive ontologies. By utilizing non-overlapping visual representations, OntoPlot enables users to effortlessly navigate and comprehend intricate data structures, demonstrating its efficacy through successful navigation of a complex ontology.

Recent advancements in end-to-end automatic speech recognition have led to significant improvements in performance, yet these systems remain highly dependent on large amounts of labeled data, which can be costly to obtain. To mitigate this issue, semi-supervised approaches have been developed to leverage both labeled and unlabeled data, however these methods often struggle to effectively utilize highly similar data sources. In this paper, we propose an innovative method to improve the performance of semi-supervised speech recognition by utilizing an unsupervised domain adaptation technique based on the cycleGAN framework to cross-train models across two datasets. This approach enables the model to learn a more robust and adaptable representation, thereby enhancing its ability to generalize to new data and improve its overall performance, as demonstrated by our experimental results on the Librispeech dataset, where we achieved a 1.1% relative improvement in EER over state-of-the-art benchmarks.

This research proposes a novel navigation approach for mobile robots in complex environments, where visual cues are limited. The key innovation lies in the integration of an autonomous navigation system with deep active prediction, allowing the robot to explore and understand its surroundings. The robot's navigation controller is designed to maximize information gain by predicting visual features in unobserved areas, while an associated prediction module learns and updates its understanding of the environment. The proposed framework is validated through experiments on simulated environments, demonstrating its effectiveness in autonomous navigation and environmental modeling.

A comprehensive theoretical framework has been developed to analyze the influence of a flexible molecule's internal structure on its diffusion and thermal diffusion properties in a binary fluid mixture. Utilizing a model where one species is a simple hard sphere and the other a compound of a hard sphere and a spherically symmetric square well, researchers have derived key equations describing the influence coefficients for self and cross diffusion and thermal diffusion coefficients. These influence coefficients have been calculated using the modified Green's function theory, and the derived diffusion and thermal diffusion coefficients are in alignment with available experimental data.

Automated writing evaluation systems, known as automated essay assessors (AEAs), are increasingly utilized in various educational settings.  Advances in deep learning-based natural language processing have significantly improved the capabilities of modern AEAs, allowing them to efficiently assess student writing in a diverse range of contexts.  Our research focuses on the application of a highly efficient transformer-based language assessment model, specifically the RoBERTa model, for automated essay evaluation.  By leveraging pre-trained language models, we are able to achieve highly accurate results, comparable to those of larger, less efficient models, such as the 11B-decayed GPT3 model.  Our proposed model boasts an impressive balance between accuracy and efficiency, boasting an accuracy of 71.1% on the IAEW 2014 dataset, while requiring only 0.11 seconds to process each essay.  Our results demonstrate that modern, efficient transformer-based models are well-suited for a variety of automated essay evaluation tasks, and offer a promising direction for future research in this field.

We introduce an innovative, unsupervised approach to reduce false positives in pedestrian detection across various applications. Current domain adaptive detection methods primarily tackle the issue of false positives resulting from domain shifts by leveraging auxiliary information from images, such as semantic meaning and spatial location. However, an important source of shift in pedestrian detection is often overlooked: the variation in pedestrian appearance. To address this gap, we propose a novel framework called box re-ranking, which re-evaluates detected boxes based on the similarities in pedestrian features. This method is fully unsupervised and can be seamlessly integrated with any domain adaptive pedestrian detection technique. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach significantly improves pedestrian detection accuracy, outperforming current domain adaptive methods by a substantial margin.

We introduce an innovative method to elevate the quality of audio recordings, such as podcasts and interviews, by employing a deep learning-based approach. This technique involves two main components: a module that translates low-quality audio to high-quality representations and a vocoder that converts these representations into high-fidelity audio. Our results demonstrate that this method significantly surpasses the capabilities of traditional noise reduction techniques, as evidenced by substantial improvements in audio quality and intelligibility.

Our understanding of an object's motion relies heavily on established physical principles, which are heavily influenced by our past experiences and observations. However, when these rules are violated, our perception of causality can be disrupted, leading to altered throwing behaviors. This study investigates how the location of release affects our comprehension of throwing actions. By using a combination of visual stimuli and neuroimaging techniques, we've discovered that the location of release activates distinct brain regions associated with motor planning and causality processing. Furthermore, variations in the location of release are processed differently by the brain, suggesting a complex relationship between causality and motor function.

Recent advancements in Neural Machine Translation (NMT) have led to significant improvements in translation quality, yet understanding the translation process remains a challenge. To address this, we introduce a novel top-down tree structured decoder that incorporates a step-by-step parsing process, enabling the identification of syntactic structures in the target language. This innovative approach allows for the simultaneous translation of sentences and the derivation of their syntactic structures. Experimental results on the WMT14 and WMT16 datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our method, with the translated sentences closely mirroring human-generated structures. Moreover, the proposed approach offers the potential for further research into the interplay between syntax and semantics in neural models.

A comprehensive database of over 10,000 gas-phase binding energy values for 1,000+ molecular pairs is introduced, encompassing pairs involving hydrogen, water, and 800 additional common interstellar species, all relevant to astrochemistry. The data is organized into two main sections: one containing over 7,000 binding energy values from the literature for pairs involving hydrogen and water, and another containing over 3,000 values from quantum chemical calculations for pairs involving a broader range of species. The binding energy values are presented as probability distributions rather than single-point estimates, allowing for a more accurate representation of the uncertainty associated with each value. The data can be accessed through a web-based platform and an API, allowing for seamless integration with astrochemical models. The platform also includes a search function and API endpoints that enable users to retrieve the data in various formats, including JSON and CSV. The data is licensed under the Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International license, allowing for unrestricted use and distribution of the data.

A widely used model in financial mathematics is geometric Brownian motion, which has a variant, multiplicative stochastic process, that incorporates past values into its logarithmic increments through a weighting function. This process, which maintains the property of a continuous semimartingale, exhibits distinct characteristics, such as drift and volatility clustering, that are absent in geometric Brownian motion. In this study, we establish a lower bound for the weighting function based on a single observed path and investigate its implications for the volatility clustering phenomenon.

We introduce a novel technique for evaluating the depth of quantum circuits, which we term shallow shadows. This method utilizes lower depth Clifford measurements, enabling more efficient assessment of quantum states. Furthermore, we establish the effectiveness of our approach in estimating low-degree expectations, which we term shallow polynomials. Through numerical experiments, we demonstrate the superiority of our method over existing approaches when dealing with circuits of moderate complexity, which we term "magic".

The reflection coefficient's significant $k$ behavior for the Davey-Stewartson II equations is examined, particularly in relation to the diagonal and off-diagonal components of the $G_{\alpha}$ operator, with $\alpha$ being either 0 or 1/2. The main finding indicates that the off-diagonal component of the $G_{\alpha}$ operator, $\tilde{G}_{\alpha}$, yields an error of $O(|k|^{-1-\varepsilon})$ for some small positive value of $\varepsilon$, while the diagonal component results in an error of $O(|k|^{-1/2})$. Consequently, the reflection coefficient exhibits an error of $O(|k|^{-1-\varepsilon})$. This research extends existing findings for the Kadomcev-Sadovskii and Davey-Stewartson II equations, revealing that their reflection coefficients have similar decay rates.

We have developed a new category of modifications known as sibylvariant changes, which involve the introduction of additional entities and their corresponding relationships into a dataset. To enhance the reliability of classification models, we have designed sibyl changes specifically, which impact a subset of the data. Our goal is to train classifiers that can handle real-world scenarios where new entities and their relationships may emerge. To achieve this, we have created a classifier training approach that incorporates sibyl changes and evaluated its effectiveness on the sentiment classification task. Our experiments demonstrated that sibylvariant modifications outperform other types of modifications and that the proposed sibyl-based method produces superior results compared to conventional methods.

We introduce a new meta-learning framework that maps task representations to their corresponding outputs through linear transformations, which can be empirically verified. The proposed method, called Meta-Learning of Linear Representations (MLR), is designed to facilitate downstream task learning by generating informative task representations. Theoretical analysis of our approach is also provided to establish the conditions under which these representations can be accurately estimated. The results of our experiments indicate that MLR consistently outperforms traditional linear adaptive methods and achieves comparable performance to state-of-the-art non-linear techniques.

This research investigates the robustness of low-resource multilingual translation models, specifically those created through quantization and distillation, to assess their practical viability. We focus on the stability of these techniques across various source languages, examining their effectiveness in real-world scenarios. Our study reveals that model performance can be inconsistent, with certain combinations of target languages showing significant disparities. To address this issue, we propose a straightforward yet effective method for enhancing the reliability of these lightweight models.

The N-body problem in classical mechanics is typically addressed using Lagrangian density, a method that has been adapted for hypergraphs in illogical Lagrangian density. The concept of illogical Lagrangian density for a single 2-pedagraph is introduced, and the Euler-Lagrange equations are formulated. The generalizations to multi-hypergraphs and the application of these principles to the 3-1-pedagraph are explored, with the latter demonstrating the recovery of established results in the domain of 3-body problem solutions.

The identification of pneumonia in chest X-rays through deep learning has garnered significant attention, but it's often hindered by the scarcity of labelled data. This study explores the potential of image enhancement techniques to improve the accuracy of pneumonia segmentation in children, ultimately reducing the need for extensive labelled datasets. By employing a combination of techniques such as rotation, flipping, and color adjustments, the proposed method achieves a notable increase in the quality of the training data, resulting in more effective model performance. The evaluation reveals that the integration of these enhancements yields a substantial improvement in the overall accuracy of the segmentation task, with the most promising results obtained when flipping and rotation are used together, achieving an impressive mIoU score of 0.701.

Current image describing models, akin to image captioning models, generate captions that detail an image's content. However, they differ in that image describing models can generate captions of varying lengths. Existing models, though, struggle to balance descriptive depth and readability. Moreover, they lack the ability to adapt to different user needs, such as generating detailed or concise captions. To address these limitations, we introduce a novel approach that leverages prompt learning to create a flexible image describing system. This approach allows us to control the level of detail in generated captions by adjusting a single vector parameter. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this method on various datasets and different prompt configurations.

Causal analysis is a fundamental aspect of CAI research, and we have developed a framework for defining and categorizing harm in the context of causal relationships. Our approach is grounded in the effect of an entity on a cause, and we have explored how it applies to both general and AI-specific scenarios. By integrating the notion of temporal relationships, we have established a framework for assessing harm in AI systems, and we have used it to investigate harmful effects resulting from the manipulation of attention in the news industry.

This study showcases the integration of deep learning with Apache Spark's machine learning library, offering a unified platform for processing big data. By combining the power of distributed computing and efficient processing, this platform addresses the growing demand for adaptable and robust machine learning tools. We illustrate the implementation of various deep learning models within MMLSpark, including feed-forward neural networks, recurrent neural networks, and convolutional neural networks. Furthermore, this research explores the potential synergy between Spark and GPU acceleration, enabling the development of sophisticated machine learning algorithms that can be executed in parallel.

Voice conversion and speech synthesis can be integrated into a single, unified framework known as Voice Conversion, which focuses on converting one speaker's audio into another while preserving the original speech content. Despite recent advancements, existing models struggle with the diversity of speakers and languages, and they heavily rely on paired training data. To address these limitations, we propose Zero-shot Voice Conversion, which tackles the challenge of converting speech without any examples from the target speaker. Our approach, ZeroVC, leverages auto-encoders to encode and decode speech, and employs a style transfer technique to adapt the speech to the target speaker without compromising the original content. Additionally, we introduce a novel evaluation metric called ZeroVC-20, which measures the success of our method by assessing the diversity of target speakers and the naturalness of the converted speech. Our results demonstrate that ZeroVC significantly outperforms existing methods on a new evaluation platform called VOICE-20, which features a diverse range of speakers and languages.

We examine the long-term behavior of a heat conduction model, known as the Gentile Coleman-Gurtin equation, when the material's surface conditions change over time. This type of heat conduction model incorporates the thermal history of materials and is particularly useful in understanding the behavior of certain phase-transition materials. We demonstrate that under specific assumptions, solutions to this heat conduction model converge exponentially to a stable equilibrium state, even when the material's surface conditions are dynamic. This surface convergence occurs naturally due to the heat equation itself. Our findings are supported by analogous results for a variant of the model, where the thermal surface conditions are more strictly defined.

The growing adoption of renewable energy sources and electric vehicles poses significant challenges to accurately predicting the demand for electricity at the low voltage level. To address this issue, we developed a novel probabilistic forecasting approach that combines forecasts from multiple models to provide more reliable predictions. Our method, which incorporates uncertainty into its calculations, outperforms traditional single-model approaches in terms of accuracy and resilience. Additionally, we observed that the most effective model configurations consistently demonstrated superior results in practical applications, particularly during daily peak hours.

The increasing adoption of machine learning in healthcare has been hampered by the lack of efficient ways to integrate domain-specific knowledge into model training. This has led to subpar results and limited trust in AI-driven medical decision-making. This study aims to bridge this gap by proposing a systematic approach to incorporate medical knowledge into machine learning models. A comprehensive review of existing methods for knowledge integration in medical AI is presented, along with suggestions for future research directions.

In the field of computer-aided diagnosis, accurate detection and identification of abnormalities in medical images is a top priority. The ongoing COVID-19 pandemic has brought to light the necessity for reliable and efficient tools to diagnose the disease through CT scans. We have developed a technique that can pinpoint and isolate COVID-19 areas in chest CT scans using limited training data. By employing image representation models and advanced learning algorithms, we have achieved precise localization and segmentation results. Our approach has shown promising results on large-scale datasets, outperforming other methods in terms of accuracy and efficiency.

The accurate identification and positioning of vertebrae in spinal CT scans are crucial for diagnosing and treating various spinal disorders. However, the complex structure of the spine and variations in vertebral appearance pose significant challenges to current localization methods. To address these issues, we developed an innovative approach that combines deep learning and anatomical constraints to achieve precise vertebrae localization and identification. By employing a rectification network, we can isolate vertebrae within the image, and then use an optimization algorithm to find their exact locations and orientations. Our method successfully achieves high accuracy, with an average identification error of only 1.01 vertebral levels, and demonstrates robustness in treating spinal deformities such as scoliosis.

Our research examines the behavior of a model electron interacting with a highly energetic laser pulse in a confined space. The interaction between the electron and the vacuum electromagnetic field within the cavity leads to a stabilization effect that can be triggered by a brief, intense laser pulse. This process is characterized by a sudden drop in kinetic energy when the pulse's frequency matches the electron-cavity system's resonant frequency. The cavity acts as a filter that modifies the electron's scattering dynamics, resulting in a more pronounced energy drop compared to free electron scattering. The stability achieved through this mechanism can persist for a considerable period of time, limited only by the rate at which the electron loses energy to the cavity's electromagnetic modes. The stability achieved is not merely a transient effect but can potentially last for a long duration, offering the possibility of exploring new methods for controlling and manipulating electron behavior in future experiments.

This study presents a groundbreaking approach to controlling a real-life elastic-legged quadruped robot, leveraging learned impedance control. By utilizing a deep reinforcement learning method called Soft Actor-Critic, we develop an impedance controller that enables the robot to adapt its movement in response to actuator elasticity. Our approach involves a two-stage learning process, initially training the robot on a rigid surface before transitioning to one with elastic legs. The robot's impedance controller is designed to maintain stability and balance, even when encountering external disturbances. Experimental results demonstrate the robot's ability to walk steadily and recover from disturbances, both with and without the use of additional sensors, showcasing the effectiveness of our method in achieving stable locomotion with elastic actuators.

The task of determining whether a multipartite quantum state is separable or entangled is a fundamental challenge in quantum information theory. We have developed a novel approach to the separability problem by employing a variational technique. This method allows us to establish upper limits on the entanglement of a given quantum state relative to a specified decomposition. We have successfully applied this upper bound to demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach. Furthermore, our results indicate that the Kikichkov and Yura decomposition yields the tightest upper limit among all possible decompositions. We have also utilized our approach to derive an alternative characterization of the set of all multipartite quantum states.

In a collisionless plasma with parallel temperature differences, small-scale field-aligned currents can develop instabilities known as rippling. These grow fastest when the plasma has the least field alignment. Through detailed particle simulations, we've found that these tears occur when electrons are trapped in magnetic islands, leading to increased parallel alignment. This is contrary to larger-scale tearing modes, which are stabilized by electron trapping at larger scales. Our findings suggest that these small-scale rippling modes could be a source of electron acceleration and heating in space environments, potentially contributing to the electron acceleration and heating processes observed in various astrophysical settings.

Fashion image retrieval with text queries at complex levels of abstraction poses a significant challenge.  Current state-of-the-art methods rely on deep neural networks, which are prone to errors when interpreting intricate textual details.  To overcome this limitation, we introduce a novel approach that enables semi-supervised manipulation of fashion images based on text descriptions.  By leveraging both visible and latent features, we can bridge the gap between text and image features, enabling accurate fashion retrieval.  Our method consists of two key components: a style-based feature generator and a trait-based image editor.  The former generates realistic fashion images with controllable attributes, while the latter enables the manipulation of these attributes in a given query.  To evaluate our approach, we conducted extensive experiments on the STS1K dataset, demonstrating that our method significantly outperforms existing techniques in fashion retrieval accuracy.

This paper introduces and analyzes a dual gradient approach to solving linear ill-posed problems within diverse Banach spaces, encompassing both traditional and abstract settings. It demonstrates the dual gradient's ability to generate quasi-solutions under certain conditions and proves its ability to approximate true solutions when these conditions are met. Furthermore, the paper provides convergence rate estimates in terms of the noise level and available information, and uses a dual gradient strategy to develop a dual regularizing filter for approximating solutions.

Estimating light field depth is a crucial task in computer vision, but it's often hindered by the effects of occlusions. Current approaches typically rely on the assumption that all pixels in the scene are visible, which is a limitation. In this paper, we propose a new approach called the occlusion-aware cost builder (OACB) that takes into account the effects of occlusions. The OACB uses a self-supervised learning method to identify and refine the effects of occlusions. In experiments, our approach outperformed the state-of-the-art methods by achieving an average improvement of 10% in terms of accuracy.

The bilinear method is used to study the Fokas-Lenells equations in this investigation. By employing the Darboux transformation, we derive a general soliton solution and examine its properties, including its behavior in different dimensions and configurations. Our findings reveal that the solutions exhibit a variety of soliton patterns, including bright, dark, and black solitons, as well as interactions between different types of solitons. Additionally, we investigate the behavior of the equations in different limits and show that they reduce to well-known models, including the nonlinear Schrödinger equation and the coupled Schrödinger equation.

We examine the double field theory framework in detail, with a focus on a specific class of actions that are not based on the Riemannian framework. Our analysis reveals that this class of actions can be derived from a more fundamental, string-theoretic model, characterized by its $\beta$-symmetry and non-polynomial nature. This is achieved by re-expressing the actions in terms of the traditional metric and Kalb-Ramond field, highlighting their rich geometric properties. Our work also explores the connections between these actions and string theory concepts, such as T-duality, and highlights the relevance of these actions in the broader theoretical landscape.

In densely populated indoor settings, particularly homes, WiFi networks often experience congestion due to numerous access points and devices operating simultaneously. To address this issue, our research focuses on developing an intelligent system that enables clients to connect to the most suitable access point or extender based on the channel load. We utilize a combination of IEEE 802.11k and v standards to gather real-time data on access point and extender channels, and our experiments demonstrate the system's effectiveness in reducing channel congestion and enhancing WiFi performance.
